subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 14! In this unit you will become confident with two of the most useful measurements in all of mathematics: perimeter and area. Perimeter is the distance all the way around the outside of a shape, and area is the amount of flat space inside it. These two ideas may sound similar, but they answer very different questions, and telling them apart is one of the key skills you will master here.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 4 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Explain the difference between area and perimeter in your own words.
Measure and calculate perimeter using linear units (mm, cm, m, km).
Measure and calculate area using square units (mm², cm², m², km²).
Estimate the area of a shape by counting whole and partial squares.
Use the formulas for the perimeter and area of rectangles and squares.
Choose the most sensible unit for measuring a given object.
Convert between different units of length and of area.
Find the area of a compound shape by splitting it into rectangles.
Solve real-world problems involving area and perimeter.
Use standard units of mass (g, kg) and capacity (ml, l), know the relationships between them (1 kg = 1,000 g and 1 l = 1,000 ml), and read a scale that is only partly numbered.

concepts.title: What Perimeter Really Means
concepts.explanation:
Perimeter is the distance all the way around the outside edge of a flat shape. Imagine a tiny ant walking around the very edge of the shape until it returns to where it started. The total distance that ant walks is the perimeter. Because perimeter is a distance, it is a length, and we measure it in ordinary linear units such as millimetres (mm), centimetres (cm), metres (m) or kilometres (km).

To find the perimeter of any straight-sided shape, you simply add up the lengths of all its sides. Nothing more clever than that is needed. If a triangle has sides of 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm, its perimeter is 3 + 4 + 5 = 12 cm. If a five-sided shape has sides of 2 m, 2 m, 3 m, 1 m and 4 m, its perimeter is 2 + 2 + 3 + 1 + 4 = 12 m.

Think of the real reasons you might need a perimeter. When Hassan fences the goat pen, the amount of fencing wire he must buy is exactly the perimeter of the pen. When Khadija sews a decorative border around the edge of a prayer mat, the length of ribbon she needs is the perimeter of the mat. Whenever the question is about going around the edge – fencing, framing, bordering, or a running track around a field – you are dealing with perimeter.
concepts.example: Here is a picture to hold in your mind. Suppose a rectangular garden has sides of 5 m, 3 m, 5 m and 3 m. Starting at one corner, the ant walks 5 m along the top, then 3 m down the side, then 5 m back along the bottom, then 3 m up the last side, arriving home. Adding those legs of the journey: 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 m. The perimeter of the garden is 16 m, and that is how much fencing Hassan would need to enclose it.

concepts.title: What Area Really Means
concepts.explanation:
Area is the amount of flat space inside a shape – how much surface it covers. Instead of walking around the edge like the ant, imagine covering the whole inside of the shape with small identical squares, leaving no gaps and no overlaps. The number of squares it takes to cover the shape is its area. Because area is measured in squares, we use square units: square millimetres (mm²), square centimetres (cm²), square metres (m²) or square kilometres (km²).

The little ² after the unit is important. It is read as squared and it reminds everyone that we are counting squares, not lengths. Writing 15 cm² means fifteen little one-centimetre squares fit inside the shape. Writing just 15 cm would mean a length of fifteen centimetres – a completely different thing. Never drop the ², because the ² is the difference between area and length.

Think of the real reasons you might need an area. When Amina lays a mat to cover a floor, the size of mat she needs is the area of the floor. When Yusuf paints a wall, the amount of paint depends on the area of the wall. When a farmer plants seeds evenly across a field, the number of seeds depends on the area of the field. Whenever the question is about covering a surface – carpeting, painting, tiling, planting – you are dealing with area.
concepts.example: Picture a rectangle that is 5 cm long and 3 cm wide, drawn on squared paper. You could cover it with little one-centimetre squares arranged in 3 rows of 5 squares. Counting them all gives 15 squares, so the area is 15 cm². Notice that 3 rows of 5 is simply 5 × 3 = 15 – which is why, as you will see next, we can find the area of a rectangle by multiplying instead of counting every square one by one.

concepts.title: Telling Area and Perimeter Apart
concepts.explanation:
This is the idea that separates confident learners from confused ones, so let us make it crystal clear. Perimeter and area answer different questions about the same shape:

Perimeter asks: how far is it around the edge? It is a length, measured in mm, cm, m or km.

Area asks: how much space is inside? It is a covering of squares, measured in mm², cm², m² or km².

A powerful way to see the difference is to notice a surprising fact: two shapes can have the same perimeter but different areas, and two shapes can have the same area but different perimeters. They are truly independent measurements. Let us look at both surprises, because understanding them will lift your thinking above simple copying of formulas.

Same area, different perimeter. Think of four rectangles that all have an area of 24 square units: a 1 × 24, a 2 × 12, a 3 × 8, and a 4 × 6. Each one covers exactly 24 squares, so all four have the same area. But their perimeters are very different. The 1 × 24 has perimeter 2 × (1 + 24) = 50 units – long and thin, with a huge edge. The 4 × 6 has perimeter 2 × (4 + 6) = 20 units – short and stubby. As a rectangle of fixed area gets closer to a square shape, its perimeter shrinks.

Same perimeter, different area. Now think of rectangles that all have a perimeter of 20 units: a 1 × 9, a 2 × 8, a 3 × 7, a 4 × 6, and a 5 × 5. Each has perimeter 20, yet their areas climb from 9, to 16, to 21, to 24, and finally to 25 square units for the 5 × 5 square. So among all rectangles with the same perimeter, the square holds the most space. This is why, if Hassan has a fixed length of fencing, a square pen gives his goats the most room to move.
concepts.example: Keep these two facts close. They prove that you can never work out one measurement just by knowing the other. You must always look carefully at what the question is truly asking – around the edge, or inside the shape?

concepts.title: Choosing the Right Units
concepts.explanation:
Choosing a sensible unit is part of doing measurement well. We do not measure the distance between Mogadishu and Nairobi in millimetres, and we do not measure a postage stamp in kilometres. The unit should suit the size of the thing being measured.

For perimeter and length, use linear units:

Millimetres (mm) – for very small objects, like a coin or a bead.

Centimetres (cm) – for small objects, like a book or a plate.

Metres (m) – for larger things, like a room, a fence or a football pitch.

Kilometres (km) – for very long distances, like the boundary of a large park or the road between two towns.

For area, use the matching square units:

Square millimetres (mm²) – for very small areas, like a single stamp or a drop of water.

Square centimetres (cm²) – for small areas, like a book cover or a photograph.

Square metres (m²) – for larger areas, like the floor of a room or a garden plot.
concepts.example: Square kilometres (km²) – for very large areas, like a city, a lake or a national park.

concepts.title: Perimeter and Area of a Rectangle by Formula
concepts.explanation:
For rectangles and squares, we have neat formulas that let us find perimeter and area quickly without counting or adding every side one at a time. A formula is just a rule written with symbols that works every single time.

A rectangle has four sides, and opposite sides are equal, so there are really only two different side lengths: the length and the width. There are two easy ways to find the perimeter.

Method 1 – add all four sides: Perimeter = length + width + length + width, which is the same as 2 × length + 2 × width. Method 2 – add length and width first, then double: Perimeter = 2 × (length + width). Both methods always give the same answer; choose whichever feels easier.

For example, take a rectangle 7 cm long and 4 cm wide. Using Method 2: Perimeter = 2 × (7 + 4) = 2 × 11 = 22 cm. Using Method 1 as a check: 7 + 4 + 7 + 4 = 22 cm. The two methods agree, which tells us the answer is right.

The area of a rectangle is found by multiplying its length by its width: Area = length × width. This works because the length tells you how many squares fit in one row, and the width tells you how many rows there are, so multiplying gives the total number of squares.

For example, take that same rectangle 7 cm long and 4 cm wide. Area = 7 × 4 = 28 cm². There are 4 rows with 7 squares in each row, and 4 sevens make 28. Notice again that area comes with a square unit (cm²) while perimeter comes with a plain length unit (cm).

A square has all four sides equal, so its formulas are even simpler. If each side is s, then Perimeter = 4 × s and Area = s × s. For a square with sides of 6 cm: Perimeter = 4 × 6 = 24 cm, and Area = 6 × 6 = 36 cm².
concepts.example: ⭐ Rectangle Formulas Perimeter = 2 x (length + width). Area = length x width. Square: Perimeter = 4 x side. Area = side x side. Perimeter uses length units. Area uses square units. Never mix them up.

concepts.title: Finding a Missing Side
concepts.explanation:
Sometimes a problem gives you the perimeter or area and one side, and asks you to work backwards to find the missing side. This is where understanding the formulas – rather than just memorising them – really pays off.

Missing side from perimeter. Suppose a rectangle has a perimeter of 24 cm and a length of 7 cm. We know 2 × (length + width) = 24, so length + width = 12. Since the length is 7, the width must be 12 − 7 = 5 cm. A quick way to think about it: half the perimeter is always one length plus one width, so take half the perimeter and subtract the side you know.

Missing side from area. Suppose a rectangle has an area of 24 cm² and a length of 6 cm. We know length × width = 24, so 6 × width = 24. We ask what times 6 makes 24, and the answer is 4, so the width is 4 cm. Finding a missing side from area is really a division: width = area ÷ length.
concepts.example: The same idea helps with squares. If a square has a perimeter of 36 cm, then since all four sides are equal, each side is 36 ÷ 4 = 9 cm. If a square has an area of 49 cm², then since area is side × side, we ask what number times itself makes 49, and the answer is 7, so each side is 7 cm.

concepts.title: Mass and Capacity: Standard Units
concepts.explanation: So far in this unit you have measured length, but there are two more kinds of measurement you will use throughout Year 4: mass (how heavy something is) and capacity (how much liquid something holds). Mass is measured in grams (g) and kilograms (kg). A gram is very light — a paperclip has a mass of about one gram. A kilogram is 1,000 grams, and it is a sensible unit for heavier things such as a bag of rice, a goat, or a young child. The word 'kilo' means 'one thousand', the very same 'kilo' you already know from kilometres. Capacity is measured in millilitres (ml) and litres (l). A millilitre is a tiny amount — about 20 drops of water fill one millilitre. A litre is 1,000 millilitres, and it is a sensible unit for things such as a bottle of water or a bucket. The word 'milli' means 'one thousandth', the very same 'milli' you already know from millimetres. Just as with length, choose the smaller unit (g or ml) for small amounts and the larger unit (kg or l) for large amounts, so your numbers stay sensible to read and write.
concepts.example: 1 kg = 1,000 g, so 3 kg = 3,000 g, and 2,500 g = 2.5 kg (divide by 1,000 to change grams to kilograms). In the same way, 1 l = 1,000 ml, so 4 l = 4,000 ml, and 1,500 ml = 1.5 l. To read a scale that is only partly numbered (like a kitchen scale or a measuring jug where only some marks show a number), first work out what one small gap is worth: find two numbered marks, count the equal gaps between them, and divide. For example, if 0 kg and 1 kg are marked with 5 equal gaps between them, each small gap is worth 1,000 g ÷ 5 = 200 g, so you can read any unmarked line by counting gaps from a numbered one.

methods.title: How to find area and perimeter of a rectangle
methods.example: Find the perimeter of a rectangle that is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide.
steps: Read off the length and the width, with their units.
For perimeter, add length and width, then double.
For area, multiply length by width.
Write each answer with the correct unit — a plain unit for perimeter, a square unit for area.

methods.title: How to find a missing side
methods.example: Find the area of a rectangle that is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide.
steps: From perimeter: halve the perimeter, then subtract the side you know.
From area: divide the area by the side you know.
Check your answer by putting it back into the formula.

methods.title: How to find the area of a compound shape
methods.example: A square tile has sides of 9 cm. Find its perimeter and its area.
steps: Split the shape into rectangles with a straight line.
Find the length and width of each rectangle.
Find each area with length × width.
Add all the areas together.

methods.title: Finding a missing width from perimeter
methods.example: A rectangle has a perimeter of 30 m and a width of 5 m. What is its length?
steps: Half the perimeter is one length plus one width: 30 ÷ 2 = 15 m.
Take away the width: 15 − 5 = 10 m.
Correct.

methods.title: Finding a missing width from area
methods.example: A rectangle has an area of 35 m² and a width of 5 m. What is its length?
steps: Since Area = length × width, we have length × 5 = 35.
Divide: length = 35 ÷ 5 = 7 m.
Check: 7 × 5 = 35 m².
Correct.

methods.title: Estimating area by counting squares
methods.example: A spilled patch of water on squared paper covers 10 whole squares and 6 squares that are each more than half filled. Estimate its area.
steps: Count each more-than-half square as one: 10 + 6 = about 16 square units.
This is an estimate, because the part squares are judged by eye.
Check your estimate is reasonable by comparing it to the total number of squares in the grid.

workedExamples.title: Perimeter of a rectangle
workedExamples.prompt: Find the perimeter of a rectangle that is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide.
workedExamples.solution: Use Perimeter = 2 × (length + width) = 2 × (8 + 5) = 2 × 13 = 26 cm. Check by adding all four sides: 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 cm. The answer uses cm because perimeter is a length.

workedExamples.title: Area of a rectangle
workedExamples.prompt: Find the area of a rectangle that is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide.
workedExamples.solution: Use Area = length × width = 8 × 5 = 40 cm². Picture 5 rows with 8 squares in each row: 5 eights make 40. The answer uses cm² because area is measured in squares.

workedExamples.title: Perimeter and area of a square
workedExamples.prompt: A square tile has sides of 9 cm. Find its perimeter and its area.
workedExamples.solution: Perimeter = 4 × side = 4 × 9 = 36 cm. Area = side × side = 9 × 9 = 81 cm². Notice how the two answers have very different sizes and different units, even though they come from the same square.

workedExamples.title: Finding a missing width from perimeter
workedExamples.prompt: A rectangle has a perimeter of 30 m and a width of 5 m. What is its length?
workedExamples.solution: Half the perimeter is one length plus one width: 30 ÷ 2 = 15 m. Take away the width: 15 − 5 = 10 m. Check: 2 × (10 + 5) = 2 × 15 = 30 m. Correct.

workedExamples.title: Finding a missing width from area
workedExamples.prompt: A rectangle has an area of 35 m² and a width of 5 m. What is its length?
workedExamples.solution: Since Area = length × width, we have length × 5 = 35. Divide: length = 35 ÷ 5 = 7 m. Check: 7 × 5 = 35 m². Correct.

workedExamples.title: Estimating area by counting squares
workedExamples.prompt: A spilled patch of water on squared paper covers 10 whole squares and 6 squares that are each more than half filled. Estimate its area.
workedExamples.solution: Count each more-than-half square as one: 10 + 6 = about 16 square units. This is an estimate, because the part squares are judged by eye.

workedExamples.title: Area of a compound shape
workedExamples.prompt: An L-shaped floor splits into a 6 m × 4 m rectangle and a 3 m × 2 m rectangle. Find the total area.
workedExamples.solution: Rectangle 1: 6 × 4 = 24 m². Rectangle 2: 3 × 2 = 6 m². Add them: 24 + 6 = 30 m². That is how much matting would cover the whole floor.

workedExamples.title: A converting problem
workedExamples.prompt: A garden fence is 7 m long. How many centimetres is that? And if a room has an area of 4 m², how many cm² is that?
workedExamples.solution: For length, multiply by 100: 7 m = 7 × 100 = 700 cm. For area, multiply by 100 × 100 = 10 000: 4 m² = 4 × 10 000 = 40 000 cm². Length uses 100; area uses 100 squared, which is 10 000.

workedExamples.title: Practice 9
workedExamples.prompt: A rectangle has an area of 24 cm² and a length of 6 cm. Find its width.
workedExamples.solution: Area = length × width, so width = 24 ÷ 6 = 4 cm. Check: 6 × 4 = 24 cm².

workedExamples.title: Practice 10
workedExamples.prompt: Convert: a) 5 m to cm b) 250 cm to m c) 3 km to m.

workedExamples.title: Practice 11
workedExamples.prompt: Convert: a) 7 m² to cm² b) 3000 mm² to cm².
workedExamples.solution: a) 7 m² = 7 × 10,000 = 70,000 cm². b) 3,000 mm² = 3,000 ÷ 100 = 30 cm² (dividing by 100, since 1 cm² = 100 mm²).

workedExamples.title: Practice 12
workedExamples.prompt: Five rectangles all have a perimeter of 24 units: 10 × 2, 9 × 3, 8 × 4, 7 × 5 and 6 × 6. Find the area of each. Which has the largest area, and what do you notice?
workedExamples.solution: 1) Areas: 10 × 2 = 20, 9 × 3 = 27, 8 × 4 = 32, 7 × 5 = 35, 6 × 6 = 36 square units. The 6 × 6 square has the largest area — for a fixed perimeter, the square holds the most space.

activities.title: Measure Your Room (Household Objects)
activities.materials: a tape measure or a metre ruler, paper, a pencil.
steps: Choose a rectangular room, mat or table top.
Measure the length and the width, and write them down with their units.
Work out the perimeter using 2 × (length + width).
Work out the area using length × width, and write the answer with a square unit.
Measure two more objects and record all your results in a neat table.

activities.title: Squared-Paper Rectangles
activities.materials: squared paper, a pencil, a ruler.
steps: Draw a rectangle 5 squares long and 3 squares wide.
Count the squares inside to find the area, then check with 5 × 3.
Count around the edge to find the perimeter, then check with 2 × (5 + 3).
Draw three more rectangles of different sizes and do the same.
Colour the perimeter of each rectangle in one colour and shade the area in another.

activities.title: The Same-Area Challenge (Math Game)
activities.materials: squared paper and a pencil, one or two players.
steps: Agree on a target area, for example 24 squares.
Each player draws as many different rectangles with that exact area as they can (for example 1 × 24, 2 × 12, 3 × 8, 4 × 6).
Work out the perimeter of each rectangle you drew.
The player who found the rectangle with the smallest perimeter wins the round.
Talk about why the most square-like rectangle wins every time.

activities.title: Estimate the Leaf (Investigation)
activities.materials: squared paper, a leaf or a flat stone, a pencil.
steps: Place the leaf on the squared paper and draw around its edge.
Estimate the area first – make a sensible guess in squares.
Count the whole squares inside your outline.
Count the part squares that are more than half covered, and add them on.
Compare your careful count with your first estimate. How close were you?

activities.title: Design a Garden (Family Task)
activities.materials: squared paper, coloured pencils, your family's ideas.
steps: Let each square stand for 1 metre by 1 metre of ground.
Design a rectangular or L-shaped garden on the paper.
Work out the perimeter, so you know how much fencing to buy.
Work out the area, so you know how much space there is for planting.
Split any L-shape into two rectangles to find its area, then add them.

activities.title: Compound-Shape Floor Plan
activities.materials: squared paper, a ruler, a pencil.
steps: Draw an L-shaped or T-shaped room on the squared paper.
Cut the shape into two rectangles with a single straight line.
Find the area of each rectangle and add them for the total area.
Trace right around the outside to find the perimeter, counting every edge.
Swap plans with a partner and check each other's totals.

rules.title: Rectangle and Square Formulas
rules.text: For rectangles and squares, we have neat formulas that let us find perimeter and area quickly without counting or adding every side one at a time. A formula is just a rule written with symbols that works every single time.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Perimeter and Area of a Rectangle by Formula.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: For rectangles and squares, we have neat formulas that let us find perimeter and area quickly without counting or adding every side one at a time. A formula is just a rule written with symbols that works every single time. A rectangle has four sides, and opposite sides are equal, so there are really only two different side lengths: the length and the width. There are two easy ways to find the perimeter.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Finding a Missing Side.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
Sometimes a problem gives you the perimeter or area and one side, and asks you to work backwards to find the missing side. This is where understanding the formulas – rather than just memorising them – really pays off.

Missing side from perimeter. Suppose a rectangle has a perimeter of 24 cm and a length of 7 cm. We know 2 × (length + width) = 24, so length + width = 12. Since the length is 7, the width must be 12 − 7 = 5 cm. A quick way to think about it: half the perimeter is always one length plus one width, so take half the perimeter and subtract the side you know.

rounds.clue: Rectangle 1: 5 × 3 = 15 m². Rectangle 2: 2 × 4 = 8 m². Total area = 15 + 8 = 23 m².

games.title: Unit Champion: Square unit
games.description: Practise square unit through four short challenges.

rounds.prompt: What does “Linear unit” mean?
choices: A length unit: mm, cm, m, km
An area unit: mm², cm², m², km²
Four sides, four right angles, opposite sides equal
A rectangle with all four sides equal
rounds.answer: A length unit: mm, cm, m, km
rounds.clue: Use the Unit 14 Math Words & Symbols reference.
rounds.explanation: Linear unit means A length unit: mm, cm, m, km.

rounds.prompt: A rectangle is 6 cm wide and 5 cm tall. What is its area in square centimetres?
rounds.answer: Work it out step by step, then check each option.
rounds.clue: Area = width × height = 6 × 5 = 30 cm².

rounds.prompt: Which unit would be most sensible for measuring the area of a classroom floor?
choices: m²
mm²
km²
cm
rounds.answer: Think about the size of a classroom compared with each unit.
rounds.clue: A classroom floor is a moderate-sized area, so square metres (m²) is sensible. Square millimetres would be far too small, square kilometres far too large, and cm is not even an area unit.

rounds.prompt: A rectangular sports pitch is 40 m long and 25 m wide. How many metres of fencing are needed to go all the way around it?
rounds.answer: This asks for the distance around the pitch — perimeter, not area.
rounds.clue: Perimeter = 2 × (length + width) = 2 × (40 + 25) = 2 × 65 = 130 m.

selfAssessment: I can explain the difference between area and perimeter in your own words.
I can measure and calculate perimeter using linear units (mm, cm, m, km).
I can measure and calculate area using square units (mm², cm², m², km²).
I can estimate the area of a shape by counting whole and partial squares.
I can use the formulas for the perimeter and area of rectangles and squares.
I can choose the most sensible unit for measuring a given object.
I can convert between different units of length and of area.
I can find the area of a compound shape by splitting it into rectangles.
